final_answer:
PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL - ATTORNEY-CLIENT COMMUNICATION / WORK PRODUCT - PREPARED AT THE DIRECTION OF COUNSEL IN CONNECTION WITH OCR CASE NO. 04-24-38712

MEMORANDUM
To: Rachel Whitmore, Partner. Re: Verdana Health Systems, Inc. - HIPAA Compliance Program Gap Analysis. Record: the eight client documents, current through the Oct. 15, 2024 incident log. Federal law (45 CFR Parts 160/164) is analyzed; state law is flagged only. Items marked [Post-2024] postdate the record.

1. BOTTOM LINE
This is a paper program: a 2019-2021 policy set that the company neither follows nor updates. Verdana's own documents (Manual, Greenleaf report, vendor tracker, incident log) admit most violations in writing, and OCR will receive them under Subpoena Categories 1, 2, 5 and 7. Penalty exposure turns on "willful neglect" (45 CFR 160.401, 160.404). Unremediated high-risk findings since 2022, BAA lapses flagged to the CCO and ignored, and three incidents in two years support that characterization. Six items cannot wait for Nov. 4.

2. TIME-CRITICAL ITEMS

2.1 Incident #3 (Pinehurst): make the breach determination now.
- The 60-day outer limit runs from discovery: the first day the breach is known, or with reasonable diligence would be known, to the entity or any workforce member or agent other than the wrongdoer (164.404(a)(2), (b)). It is not tolled while an investigation continues. From OCR's Aug. 22 notice, day 60 is Oct. 21; from the Aug. 12 complaint (the log's own "date of discovery"), it was Oct. 11. The stated reasons for delay (awaiting Pinehurst, engaging counsel) are not recognized grounds.
- A Pinehurst administrator viewing therapy notes for personal reasons fits no 164.402(1) exception. The complainant says he used the content in a custody dispute, so "low probability of compromise" cannot be shown and the burden is the company's (164.414(b)). Treat it as a breach. No four-factor assessment has been started.
- Scope is likely wider: 12 Pinehurst staff hold root access to about 2.3 million records through shared credentials, and older logs are gone. Other patients cannot be ruled out.
- Who notifies depends on role. Verdana appears to be a business associate for provider practices (VerdaChart/VerdaCare hosting), owing the covered entity notice under 164.410, likely on shorter contractual timelines (check client BAAs). The Manual's claim of covered-entity status through "VerdaCare Premium" looks doubtful, since administering plan functions ordinarily makes an entity a business associate. Identify the complainant's covered entity now.
- Pinehurst never detected or reported the events (BAA 5.1). The record shows its employee on leave only from Sept. 1, after Verdana's Aug. 28 notice; confirm credentials were revoked.

2.2 Audit logs: preserve and reconstruct.
- Logs auto-purge at 90 days. Verdana had notice Aug. 22 and the record shows no hold, so Category 3 data keeps disappearing. Issue a written hold today, suspend the purge, export all VerdaCare/VerdaChart logs, demand Pinehurst's authentication and session records (Subpoena 3(c); BAA cooperation), and engage TerraFirm through counsel to recover from Pinehurst, Crestline and Ironbridge backups.
- Sources conflict on the loss date: the GC says before "early July," the incident log says late May (as of Aug. 26), Greenleaf says April/May. Establish what was exported when the six events were found.
- 164.312(b) requires audit controls but sets no retention period; the six-year rule (164.316(b)(2)) covers required documentation, so Greenleaf's 164.530(j) citation is arguable. But Manual 11.3/20.2 and policy VHS-SEC-004 promise six years and RA-2022-03 sat open. Do not volunteer a legal concession, but the practice cannot be defended.
- Instruction 5 requires a written account of unavailable records and the retention policy. It must be exact, and no record may be altered or back-filled (18 U.S.C. 1519; 45 CFR 160.310).

2.3 Incident #2 (laptop): late and incomplete.
- The company uses Nov. 17, 2023 as discovery, but the employee knew of the theft Nov. 14 and reported it to police Nov. 15, so discovery arguably came earlier (workforce knowledge is imputed). Even from Nov. 17, day 60 was Jan. 16, 2024. HHS notice (Jan. 28) was day 72; individual notice (Feb. 3) was day 78. The file shows 24 idle days before legal review, then 14 with the GC. OCR settled a late-notice case for $475,000 (Presence Health, 2017).
- No media or substitute notice, though 3,200 patients in four states almost certainly include more than 500 residents of one state (164.406). Nov. 17, 2023 was a Friday, not "the following Monday"; verify the timeline.
- If Verdana was a business associate for the four practices, the date of its 164.410 notice to them is undocumented. State law: confirm NC notice to consumer reporting agencies (more than 1,000 persons, N.C. Gen. Stat. 75-65) and parallel SC/VA requirements; about 1,100 SSNs were exposed.
- Aggravators: encryption was a June 2022 high-risk finding; 17 of 104 laptops and about 38 legacy installations remain unencrypted; Manual 14.3 barred local PHI storage.

2.4 Incident #1 (snooping): misclassified.
- A billing employee deliberately viewed 14 charts, including a public figure's behavioral-health record, "out of curiosity." That is not good-faith access within scope (164.402(1)(i)). The "low probability" finding was verbal, with no forensics or patient contact and no written assessment, so the burden cannot be met. Notice to the 14 patients was due about June 13, 2023, and the HHS small-breach submission by Feb. 29, 2024.
- Recommend a documented four-factor assessment now and, absent a defensible low-probability finding, late notices and filing before production. The log is responsive (Category 7(b)), and self-correction mitigates (160.408).
- The root cause persists: about 215 "Clinical Support" users have unrestricted read access to all records (Greenleaf 2024-05).

2.5 ClearView de-identification (outside the subpoena; live clock).
- Three-digit ZIPs for areas of 20,000 or fewer people must be 000 (164.514(b)(2)(i)(B)); the data is therefore PHI, sent under a DUA with no BAA, with transfers continuing through Sept. 1 despite Greenleaf's Aug. 23 advice to suspend. A breach analysis is required; day 60 from Aug. 23 is Oct. 22. Suspend transfers, re-de-identify (Expert Determination or a limited data set with a compliant agreement), and recover prior datasets.

2.6 Extension. The cover letter requires written requests 10 business days before the deadline: Oct. 21. Call Investigator Kowalski this week and file by Oct. 18 proposing rolling production. Confirm what was promised in response to OCR's Aug. 22 data request (not in the record).

3. PROGRAM GAPS

3.1 Business associates (Critical; 164.502(e), 164.504(e), 164.308(b), 164.314(a)).
- Ten of 47 vendors, not nine, lack a valid BAA: five expired (NexGen 6/30/24, Ashford, Beacon, Lakeview, Summit, the oldest since 4/30/22) and five never signed (Keystone, with about 180,000 records migrated; Thornberry; Oakridge; Foxglove, with controlled-substance data; and ClearView, which the tracker counts separately). PHI flows daily, contrary to Manual 9.1. NexGen was flagged to the CCO July 10 and later with no action. Raleigh Orthopaedic (NC) paid $750,000 over a single missing BAA. Missing subcontractor BAAs also breach client contracts.
- Cure: interim BAAs within 7 days; suspend vendors that refuse; document a risk assessment for each unprotected disclosure; refresh the 2020 template and enforce the two-year review in Manual 9.3.

3.2 Pinehurst oversight (Critical; 164.308(a)(4), 164.312(a)(2)(i), (d), 164.502(b)).
- Tracker access review: root access for 12 staff, shared admin credentials, no role limits, single-factor VPN to backups, no backend MFA (RA-2022-02, open), cleartext PHI visible in the API gateway, no dual control, no vendor-side logging. Last diligence review: June 2023. Pinehurst has stalled named accounts since Aug. 28.
- The sheet admits access is "broader than operationally necessary" and is responsive to Category 2(d). Show remediation: privileged-access management, MFA, named accounts by a date certain, termination rights.
- Category 6: Verdana likely holds no Pinehurst training records and the BAA does not require them. Say so accurately and request them from Pinehurst.

3.3 Governance (High; 164.308(a)(2), 164.530(a)).
- The Security Officer role is nominal: the CTO did not know she held it and was excluded from Incident #1. Appoint a qualified, empowered officer immediately.
- Four compliance FTEs serve 1,247 employees and 2.3 million records. The CCO reports through the GC, not the Board, and 40% of his bonus depends on revenue.
- Compliance was off the Q2 and Q3 Audit Committee agendas. On Sept. 19, 2024 the Committee was told nothing in Greenleaf's report was urgent (it lists 7 Critical findings) and was not told of the OCR complaint known since Aug. 22. Director oversight exposure under Delaware law (Caremark; Marchand v. Barnhill, not verified here) follows. The GC is also a fact witness (she cleared the laptop notice, approved the Manual and BAA template, and briefed the Committee). Recommend independent counsel for the Committee, a direct CCO-Committee line, removal of the revenue bonus component, and interim healthcare-privacy leadership.

3.4 Risk analysis (Critical; 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A)-(B)). The last enterprise analysis was June 2022. Ten of 23 findings remain open, three high-risk (encryption, MFA, logs), with no tracking or risk-acceptance memoranda. Category 5 will expose this. Commission a new analysis under privilege from an assessor other than Greenleaf, which wrote the 2022 and 2024 reports. The tracker also lists Sentinel Risk Assessment Services (V-043); determine what it did.

3.5 Policies and training (High).
- Minimum necessary is written for paper only (Manual 12.2; 164.502(b), 164.514(d)). No BYOD policy covers 312 personal phones (164.310(d)). The Manual has not been reviewed since 2021 despite Manual 22.1 (164.316(b)(2)(iii)) and ignores state law in 14 states. It omits the mandatory out-of-pocket restriction (164.522(a)(1)(vi)).
- Training (164.530(b), 164.308(a)(5)): content frozen since 2021, one module for every role, new hires average 67 days (6 of 23 timely), and 112 workforce members were not trained in the last cycle.

3.6 Incident response (High; 164.308(a)(6)). The IRP (Sept. 2020) names Hargrove, was never reviewed or tested, assumes "comprehensive audit logging" that does not exist, and lacks business-associate procedures (164.410). Ridgeline's June 2024 tabletop advice produced no action. The incident log misdescribes the IRP (different categories; mismatched section cites; says the IRP omits the 60-day deadline, though IRP 5.5.1 and App. C state it). Correct it.

4. RECORD ANOMALIES BEFORE PRODUCTION
- Greenleaf's report is dated Aug. 23, 2024 yet refers to the OCR "subpoena" (issued Oct. 3) and an Aug. 31 period end; its summary counts (5C/7H/4M/2L) conflict with its matrix (7/9/2/0). Collect all versions and metadata; an undisclosed revision is an obstruction risk.
- The Greenleaf report and incident log bear privilege legends but were prepared by an audit vendor and Compliance for business and regulatory purposes. Privilege is weak; expect to produce underlying facts.
- Greenleaf relies on law that has since moved. [Post-2024] The 2024 reproductive-health rule was vacated nationwide (Purl v. HHS, N.D. Tex. June 18, 2025); the tracking bulletin's "proscribed combination" was vacated June 20, 2024 (AHA v. Becerra), though authenticated-portal tools remain a risk. The cover letter's penalty range ($63,973-$2,067,813) appears to be pre-Aug. 8, 2024; current Tier 4 is $71,162 minimum and a $2,134,831 annual cap (89 Fed. Reg. 64815). The 2025 Security Rule NPRM (mandatory MFA/encryption) is not final.

5. SUBPOENA STRATEGY
- Cooperate, produce on a rolling basis, and lead with corrected breach determinations and remediation; OCR weighs good-faith correction and prior history (160.408) and favors informal resolution (160.312).
- Cat. 1: produce the Manual and org charts as they exist, with a cover note, and updated documents separately dated. Cat. 3: produce what exists plus Pinehurst's records and the Instruction 5 statement. Cat. 4: Employee A terminated; Employee B warned; no management sanctions. Cat. 7: finish the #1 and #3 assessments first.
- Pinehurst's employee may face 42 U.S.C. 1320d-6 exposure; any referral is a decision for counsel.

6. ROADMAP
- By Oct. 18-22: hold and log export; extension call; #3 and ClearView determinations; suspend ClearView; interim BAAs; Security Officer; Pinehurst demand.
- By Nov. 4: #1 and #2 corrective notices; production with accurate retention narrative.
- 30-90 days: new risk analysis; MFA/PAM; six-year log retention; role-based access; BYOD/MDM; IRP rewrite and tabletop; Manual overhaul.
- 90-180 days: role-based training; vendor re-papering with a BAA-before-PHI gate; encrypt remaining 17 laptops and 38 installations; governance changes.
